title: When to Call the Doctor — Red Flags
hook: Most childhood illnesses are mild, but a handful of signs mean don't wait and watch — get medical help right away. Knowing them takes the guesswork out of a scary moment.
key_points: Trouble breathing — fast or grunting breaths, or sucking in under the ribs — needs urgent help.
Any fever in a baby under 3 months is treated as urgent; call a doctor promptly.
A child who is very hard to wake, floppy, or unresponsive needs emergency care.
Call 999/911 for a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, a stiff neck, a first seizure, or blue/very pale skin.
content_html: Most childhood illnesses are mild and pass with rest and fluids — but a short list of signs means you act now rather than wait and see. The NHS groups the most serious ones as reasons to call 999 (or 911 in the US) right away: a rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass against it (a possible sign of meningitis or sepsis), a stiff neck, a seizure for the first time, blue, very pale, blotchy or grey skin, or a child who won't wake up.
extra_html: Other red flags mean get urgent medical advice without delay: real difficulty breathing — fast or grunting breaths, or sucking in under the ribs — a child who is very hard to rouse, floppy, or unusually confused, and signs of dehydration like much drier nappies than usual. And one age-based rule stands on its own: any fever in a baby under three months is treated as urgent. When you're worried about a very young baby, trust that instinct and seek help. This is general guidance from the NHS, not a substitute for advice from your own clinician or emergency services.

related.title: Fever Basics for Parents
related.hook: A fever is a sign the body is fighting infection, not a disease itself — how your child looks and acts often matters more than the exact number on the thermometer.

related.title: Vomiting and Dehydration
related.hook: When a stomach bug hits, the real risk isn't the vomiting itself — it's dehydration. The goal is keeping fluids in with small, frequent sips, and knowing the signs that mean call the doctor.

flashcards.prompt: A fever in a baby younger than 3 months should be treated as:

choices.text: Normal and best left to pass on its own
A concern only if it lasts a week

flashcards.explanation_html: Young infants can become seriously unwell quickly, so any fever under 3 months of age warrants prompt medical advice.

flashcards.prompt: What does a rash that does NOT fade when you press a glass against it suggest?
flashcards.back_html: A possible serious infection like meningitis or sepsis — it's an emergency. Call 999/911 straight away, even if your child seems okay otherwise.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these breathing signs means seek urgent help?

choices.text: Fast or grunting breaths, or sucking in under the ribs to breathe
Occasional sneezing with a runny nose
Slightly noisy breathing that clears after a sneeze

flashcards.explanation_html: Visible struggle to breathe — fast or grunting breaths, or pulling in under the ribs — is a red flag that needs urgent medical attention.
